---
title: "The cIPMA procedure"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

The combined importance-performance map analysis (cIPMA) of Hauff, Richter, Sarstedt and Ringle (2024) places each predictor of a target construct on a map of importance against performance and marks the predictors that are necessary for a target level of the construct. Importance is the total effect of the predictor on the target construct in a model of partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), and performance is the mean of the latent variable scores of the predictor, rescaled to 0–100. Necessity comes from Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), which finds the level of a predictor required for a target level of the outcome (Dul 2016).

The cIPMA package computes necessity with Quantile Necessary Condition Analysis (QNCA; Deja 2026). At the tolerance `pi = 1` the QNCA frontier equals the CE-FDH ceiling of NCA, the ceiling of the published cIPMA, and the package decides necessity at `pi = 1`. A tolerance `pi < 1` lets the share `1 - pi` of the cases that attain the target level sit below the reported requirement of a predictor.

## Steps

Hauff et al. (2024, Fig. 3) organise the cIPMA in eight steps. The analyst carries out the first three steps with the theory of the study and the `seminr` package, and the cIPMA package supports the last five:

1. Specify the research objective and the theoretical background, with hypotheses in the sufficiency logic of PLS-SEM and in the necessity logic of NCA.
2. Prepare and check the data, with the indicators of each construct on one common scale, for example 1 to 5.
3. Run the PLS-SEM analysis with `estimate_pls()` and `bootstrap_model()` of `seminr`.
4. Evaluate the reliability and validity of the measurement models and check that every outer weight is positive, with `check_assumptions()`.
5. Rescale the latent variable scores to 0–100 with the theoretical minimum and maximum of each indicator, inside `cipma()`.
6. Run the necessity analysis on the rescaled scores with the empirical scope and read the bottleneck at the target level, inside `cipma()`.
7. Evaluate the PLS-SEM significance of the total effects and the effect size and p-value of necessity, with `print()` and `summary()`.
8. Draw the combined map with `plot()`.

## Data and model

The example uses the `mobi` data of `seminr`: customers of a mobile phone provider, with indicators on a scale from 1 to 10, in the European customer satisfaction index model.

```{r procedure-data}
library(cIPMA)
library(seminr)
dim(mobi)
range(unlist(mobi))
```

The 250 customers answer 24 indicators. Loyalty is the target construct, and image, expectation, quality, value, satisfaction and complaints act on loyalty directly or through other constructs.

```{r procedure-model, message = FALSE}
mm <- constructs(
  composite("Image", multi_items("IMAG", 1:5)),
  composite("Expectation", multi_items("CUEX", 1:3)),
  composite("Quality", multi_items("PERQ", 1:7)),
  composite("Value", multi_items("PERV", 1:2)),
  composite("Satisfaction", multi_items("CUSA", 1:3)),
  composite("Complaints", single_item("CUSCO")),
  composite("Loyalty", multi_items("CUSL", 1:3))
)
sm <- relationships(
  paths(from = "Image", to = c("Expectation", "Satisfaction", "Loyalty")),
  paths(from = "Expectation", to = c("Quality", "Value", "Satisfaction")),
  paths(from = "Quality", to = c("Value", "Satisfaction")),
  paths(from = "Value", to = "Satisfaction"),
  paths(from = "Satisfaction", to = c("Complaints", "Loyalty")),
  paths(from = "Complaints", to = "Loyalty")
)
pls <- estimate_pls(mobi, mm, sm)
boot <- bootstrap_model(pls, nboot = 200, cores = 1, seed = 123)
```

The example draws 200 bootstrap resamples and, inside `cipma()`, 499 permutations, which keeps the computation short. The number of bootstrap resamples is a choice of the analyst in `bootstrap_model()`, and `cipma()` draws 1999 permutations by default.

## Measurement models

Step 4 checks the measurement models with the criteria of PLS-SEM and adds the requirement of the importance-performance map analysis (IPMA): every outer weight is positive, which keeps the rescaled scores inside 0–100 (Hauff et al. 2024).

```{r procedure-assumptions}
check_assumptions(pls)
```

Every outer weight of the model is positive, and the variance inflation factors of the structural model stay below 5. The reliability check flags image, expectation and loyalty, and four heterotrait-monotrait ratios exceed 0.90. Hauff et al. (2024) ask for improvements of a measurement model that fails the assessment criteria, and the example keeps the model unchanged as a demonstration of the procedure.

## Rescaled scores, importance and performance

`cipma()` computes the rescaled latent variable scores of Hauff et al. (2024). The standardised outer weights, divided by the standard deviation of each indicator, are normalised to sum to one within each construct, and the weighted sum of the indicators, rescaled with the theoretical minimum and maximum of the indicators given in the named list `scales`, gives the score of each case on 0–100. Importance is the total effect of each predictor on the target construct, the direct effect plus every indirect effect through mediating constructs, and performance is the mean rescaled score.

The target level of loyalty is 80 on the 0–100 scale. Hauff et al. (2024) derive the target level from expert knowledge, from the standards of the field or from the aims of the project. The bottleneck uses the tolerance `pi = 0.95`.

```{r procedure-cipma}
scales <- setNames(rep(list(c(1, 10)), ncol(mobi)), names(mobi))
res <- cipma(boot, "Loyalty", mobi, scales, target_level = 80, pi = 0.95,
             B = 499, seed = 1, pls_model = pls)
res
```

Satisfaction has the largest importance, 0.521, followed by image with 0.399, and complaints has the smallest, 0.067. Performance ranges from 62.3 for value to 75.0 for quality.

## Necessity and the bottleneck

For each predictor, `cipma()` computes the CE-FDH effect size `d` of NCA on the empirical scope of the rescaled pair: the area of the empty zone in the upper-left corner of the scatter of predictor and target construct, divided by the area of the scope, the rectangle between the observed minimum and maximum of both scores. The permutation test shuffles the target construct against the predictor `B` times, recomputes the effect size at `pi = 1` on a grid of 100 outcome levels after each shuffle, and reports the share of permuted effect sizes at least as large as the observed effect size, with one added to the count and to the number of permutations. A predictor is necessary when `d` reaches 0.10 and the p-value stays below 0.05, the rule of Hauff et al. (2024) with the effect-size landmark of Dul (2016).

Image, expectation, quality and satisfaction meet the rule, with effect sizes from 0.122 to 0.151 and p-values from 0.0020 to 0.0140. A p-value of 0.0020 is the smallest value that 499 permutations report. Value and complaints miss the rule, each with `d` = 0.016, and with p-values of 0.5600 and 0.3720.

The column `Required` gives the bottleneck: the level of the predictor required for loyalty of at least 80. At `pi = 0.95` the requirement is the 5% quantile of the predictor among the successful customers, the customers with loyalty of at least 80, so the most efficient 5% of the successful customers may sit below the requirement. The column `Failing` gives the share of all customers below the required level, which Hauff et al. (2024) read as the performance of the predictor in the necessity logic. Satisfaction carries the highest requirement, 67.209, and the largest share of customers below the requirement, 29.2%. Value and complaints also carry a requirement of 44.444 at `pi = 0.95`, and the decision at `pi = 1` keeps both outside the necessary predictors.

## Results at three levels of detail

`summary(res)` adds the bootstrap p-values of the total effects, the effect size and p-value at the chosen tolerance, the number of customers below each requirement and one reading per predictor.

```{r procedure-summary}
summary(res)
```

The total effects of image, expectation, quality and satisfaction have bootstrap p-values below 0.0001, the total effect of value 0.0143 and the total effect of complaints 0.2906. The effect sizes at `pi = 0.95` range from 0.316 to 0.421 and exceed the CE-FDH effect sizes of every predictor, because the QNCA frontier at a tolerance below 1 lies on or above the CE-FDH ceiling. Effect sizes at `pi < 1` are relative to the tolerance, and the NCA landmark of 0.10 applies to the CE-FDH effect size at `pi = 1`.

`summary(res, detail = "brief")` gives the combined table with the settings, and `summary(res, detail = "full")` adds the tolerance path of the effect size and of the required level from `pi = 1.00` to `pi = 0.90` and the bottleneck table across outcome levels.

## The combined map

`plot(res)` draws the combined map of step 8: importance on the horizontal axis, performance on the vertical axis, and dashed lines at the mean importance and the mean performance of the predictors. White bubbles mark the predictors necessary at `pi = 1`, with a size given by the share of customers below the required level, and black dots mark the other predictors.

```{r procedure-map, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Combined map of the predictors of loyalty at level 80 for the mobi data. Importance is the total effect on loyalty, and performance is the mean rescaled score on 0–100. White bubbles mark the predictors necessary at pi = 1, with a size given by the share of customers below the required level at pi = 0.95; black dots mark value and complaints."}
plot(res)
```

Satisfaction, image and quality lie in the quadrant of high importance and high performance, and expectation lies in the quadrant of low importance and high performance. Value and complaints lie in the quadrant of low importance and low performance.

## References

- Deja, M. (2026). Quantile Necessary Condition Analysis: A Tolerance-Parameterized Generalization of Necessary Condition Analysis. *Quality & Quantity* (accepted for publication).
- Dul, J. (2016). Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA): Logic and methodology of "necessary but not sufficient" causality. *Organizational Research Methods*, 19(1), 10–52. <https://doi.org/10.1177/1094428115584005>
- Hauff, S., Richter, N. F., Sarstedt, M., & Ringle, C. M. (2024). Importance and performance in PLS-SEM and NCA: Introducing the combined importance-performance map analysis (cIPMA). *Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services*, 78, 103723. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jretconser.2024.103723>
